recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which method you use on ay⁴ = (x + b)⁵ and how you finish.

steps.label: Take logarithms of both sides
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both sides are powers, so logarithms turn the indices into multipliers and remove the need to make y the subject.
lines: Take a > 0, y > 0 and x + b > 0, so both sides are positive.

recall.must_convey: That logarithms are taken of both sides, giving logₑa + 4 logₑy = 5 logₑ(x + b).
accept: take logarithms on both sides
log a plus four log y equals five log of x plus b
use logarithmic differentiation because both sides are powers
rendu vaipulaki log teesukovali
the indices four and five come down as multipliers

steps.why: Making y the subject means a fourth root and two awkward differentiations. Logarithms bring the indices down and keep every line linear in the logarithms.
common_mistakes: Writing logₑ(ay⁴) as logₑa · 4 logₑy instead of logₑa + 4 logₑy.
Taking logarithms of only one side.
steps.memory_tip: A product becomes a sum and an index becomes a multiplier — that is the whole reason for taking logarithms here.

steps.label: Differentiate once
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Keep the result in the form y′/y rather than solving for y′ — the next step differentiates this quotient as it stands.
lines: Differentiate both sides with respect to x:

recall.must_convey: That differentiating gives 4y′/y = 5/(x + b), that is, y′/y = 5/[4(x + b)].
accept: differentiate both sides with respect to x
four y dash over y equals five over x plus b
log a is a constant so it differentiates to zero
log a constant kabatti zero avuthundi
keep it as y dash over y

steps.why: d/dx(logₑy) = y′/y, so the left side arrives already in the quotient form the second differentiation needs.
common_mistakes: Writing d/dx(logₑy) as 1/y and forgetting the chain-rule factor y′.
steps.memory_tip: logₑy differentiates to y′/y — the derivative of the inside always sits on top.

steps.label: Differentiate a second time
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The left side is a quotient of y′ by y, so use the quotient rule — that is where both yy″ and (y′)² come from.

recall.must_convey: That the quotient rule on y′/y gives [yy″ − (y′)²]/y², set equal to −5/[4(x + b)²].
accept: use the quotient rule on y dash over y
that gives y y double dash minus y dash squared over y squared
the right side differentiates to minus five over four x plus b squared
quotient rule vaadithe y y double dash minus y dash square vasthundi
both terms of the required result appear here

steps.why: The two terms the question asks about, yy″ and (y′)², are exactly the numerator of the quotient rule applied to y′/y. That is why this route is short.
common_mistakes: Differentiating y′/y term by term instead of using the quotient rule.
Losing the minus sign when differentiating 1/(x + b).
steps.memory_tip: The quotient rule on y′/y produces yy″ − (y′)² on top — both pieces of the required result in one move.

steps.label: Replace 1/(x + b) and finish
steps.margin_note: Last mark. x and b must not appear in the required result, so 1/(x + b) is replaced using step 2 before the final line.

recall.must_convey: That 1/(x + b) is replaced by 4y′/(5y), giving yy″ = (1/5)(y′)², that is, 5yy″ = (y′)².
accept: replace one over x plus b using the first differentiation
one over x plus b is four y dash over five y
that leaves y y double dash equal to one fifth of y dash squared
x plus b ni y dash tho replace cheyyali
multiply by five to get five y y double dash equals y dash squared
heard_as: four y dash over five y

steps.why: The required identity has no x and no b in it, so every trace of x + b must be written back in terms of y and y′ before the last line.
common_mistakes: Leaving x + b in the final answer.
steps.memory_tip: The two indices decide the answer: with 4 logₑy = 5 logₑ(x + b), the coefficient is (5 − 4)/5 = 1/5, so the 5 in 5yy″ is the index of (x + b).
